objective: By the end of this lesson you can choose the circling maneuver for the airplane's category, speed and the conditions, read every part of a circling line of minima and its notes, explain why the pattern must stay inside both the protected radius and the published visibility, teach when it is legal to leave the circling MDA and what to do when the airport is lost from sight, demonstrate and talk through a circle, and spot and fix a learner's chart, MDA, visibility and transition errors.
why: Circling is one of the most challenging maneuvers in the NAS: it is flown at low altitude, day and night, often in precipitation, and usually to a runway with no electronic vertical guidance [[29:148|IPH 4-8]]. Its obstacle protection exists only at or above the MDA and inside a radius set by category, and once below the MDA the pilot must see and avoid obstacles [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]]. The AIM asks for sound judgment and in-depth knowledge of the pilot's own capabilities and the airplane's performance to pick the exact maneuver [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20f]], and that judgment is what you have to teach.

warmup: Think first: your learner breaks out at the circling MDA with the runway in sight, needs to land the opposite way, and the wind will be a strong tailwind on downwind. Name three ways this circle can go wrong, and what you would brief before the approach to prevent each one.

key_terms.def: A maneuver the pilot starts to line up with a runway when a straight-in landing from an instrument approach is not possible or not desirable; at a towered airport only after ATC authorization and with the required visual reference to the airport [[34:324|AIM P/CG Circle-to-land maneuver]].
The MDA and visibility required for the circle-to-land maneuver, listed under each approach category [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]].
The lowest altitude, in feet MSL, to which descent is authorized on final or during circle-to-land maneuvering when no electronic glideslope is provided [[34:378|AIM P/CG Minimum descent altitude]].
The height of the MDA above the published airport elevation, published with circling minimums [[34:356|AIM P/CG Height above airport]].
A grouping by VREF, or 1.3 VSO if no VREF is specified, at maximum certificated landing weight: A, B, C, D or E [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]].
Arcs drawn from each runway end and joined by tangent lines; obstacle clearance at the MDA exists only inside it [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]].
Built before late 2012 with one fixed radius per category; identified by the absence of the C symbol on the circling line [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]].
Built after late 2012; the radius depends on category and the circling MDA, to allow for true airspeed; identified by a white C in a black square [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]] [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]].
A chart note that closes part of the circling area, described by direction from a runway; it may apply to some categories only and differ by day and night [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f1]].
An approach with no straight-in minimums, named by the navigation system and a letter, such as VOR A [[29:157|IPH 4-17]].
ATC phrase telling the pilot to circle because the runway in use is not the one the approach is aligned with; ATC may add a direction and a downwind or base leg [[34:324|AIM P/CG Circle to runway]].
Circling and non-vertically guided procedures share the same MAP, found by timing from the FAF, by a fix, a NAVAID or a waypoint [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f5]].

chunks.title: What a circling approach is and when it is used

body.p: **Exhibits instructional knowledge of the elements of a circling approach.** A circle-to-land maneuver lines the airplane up with a runway when a straight-in landing from an instrument approach is not possible or not desirable; at a towered airport it is flown only after ATC authorization and with the required visual reference to the airport [[34:324|AIM P/CG Circle-to-land maneuver]]. The CIRCLING minimums apply when it is necessary to circle the airport, maneuver for landing, or when no straight-in minimums are published [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]. The Instrument lesson IR.VI.D covers the pilot's side of this Task, and lesson FII.VIII.A covers the decision at the MDA to land straight-in, circle or go missed. This lesson adds how you teach the circle itself.

bullets: No straight-in minimums: they are published only when the final course is within 30° of the runway and a normal descent can be made from the IFR altitude; otherwise circling minimums apply [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20c]].

Circling-only procedures carry a letter instead of a runway, such as VOR A [[29:157|IPH 4-17]]. Typical reasons: final course more than 30° off the runway, a descent gradient over 400 ft/NM from the FAF to the TCH, or a runway not clearly defined [[29:151|IPH 4-11]].

Circling minimums alone do not force a circle: with the active runway in sight in time for a normal approach and a landing clearance, the pilot is not expected to circle, and should tell ATC if he wants to [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20c]].
A circle is also needed when ATC lands you on a runway the approach does not serve, as in "cleared for VOR Runway 17 approach, circle to land Runway 23" [[29:134|IPH 3-22]].

body.p: Why it is a Task of its own: the IPH calls circling one of the most challenging maneuvers in the NAS, flown at low altitude, day and night, often in precipitation that hurts visibility and depth perception, and usually to a runway with no electronic vertical guidance [[29:148|IPH 4-8]]. The AIM adds low airspeed and marginal weather [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20f]].

callout.text: Application: on the checkride the evaluator selects Tasks A and B combined with Task C, D or E, and circling approaches do not apply to helicopters (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area VIII NOTE). So the circle may or may not be the Task selected; if it is, expect it to follow a nonprecision approach you are already flying.

check.q: A learner asks why the VOR A at his home field has no runway in its title. What do you answer?
check.a: It has only circling minimums [[29:157|IPH 4-17]]; typical reasons are a final course more than 30° off the runway, a descent gradient over 400 ft/NM, or a runway not clearly defined [[29:151|IPH 4-11]]. A straight-in landing is still possible with the runway in sight in time for a normal approach and a landing clearance [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20c]].

chunks.title: Approach category: minimums for the speed you fly

body.p: Category is set by VREF, or 1.3 VSO if no VREF is specified, at maximum certificated landing weight [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]. The IPH notes that the category speeds are indicated airspeeds [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

head: Category
Speed
rows: A
Less than 91 knots [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]
B
91 knots or more but less than 121 knots [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]
C
121 knots or more but less than 141 knots [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]
D
141 knots or more but less than 166 knots [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]
E
166 knots or more [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]

bullets: An airplane is certified in only one category and may never use the minimums of a slower category [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

Faster than the top of the category: use the higher category. The AIM examples: a Category B airplane circling at 145 knots uses Category D; a Category A airplane on a straight-in at 130 knots uses Category C [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]].
Typical causes: heavy or gusty wind, icing and non-normal conditions [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]]; overweight emergency returns and inoperative flaps [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].
Why it matters most in the circle: published circling minimums protect only inside the area for the category speed, so a faster circle needs the larger area [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

body.p: **Teach it as a preflight item.** The approach speed should be calculated, its effect on the approach worked out and briefed in preflight planning, and reviewed before starting the approach [[29:149|IPH 4-9]]. Example: no VREF, VSO 60 knots, so 1.3 x 60 = 78 knots, Category A [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]. A planned 95-knot circle in gusts is a Category B speed, so the learner briefs the B line [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]].

callout.text: Category is the speed you will fly, never lower than the certified one [[29:148|IPH 4-8]] [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]].

check.q: Your Category A learner's flaps fail and the no-flap approach speed he plans is 100 knots. Which circling line does he use?
check.a: Category B: 100 knots is in the 91 to under 121 knot range [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]], and inoperative flaps are a listed reason for higher category minimums [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

chunks.title: The circling protected area: standard and expanded

body.p: The protected area is drawn with arcs from each runway end joined by tangent lines [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]]. Inside it, at or above the MDA, the circling minimums give at least 300 ft of obstacle clearance [[29:149|IPH 4-9]] [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]. The pilot must maneuver within it to get the obstacle and terrain clearance the design provides [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7a]].

head: Area
How to tell
Radius
rows: Standard
Built before late 2012; no C symbol on the circling line [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]]
By category only, at all altitudes: A 1.3, B 1.5, C 1.7, D 2.3, E 4.5 NM [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]]
Expanded
Built after late 2012; a white C in a black square (the "negative C") on the circling line [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]]
By category and circling MDA, to allow for higher true airspeed. MDA 1,000 ft or less: A 1.3, B 1.7, C 2.7, D 3.6 NM; 1,001 to 3,000 ft: A 1.3, B 1.8, C 2.8, D 3.7 NM [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]]

body.p: Why the change matters: under the newer criteria the IPH example, a sea-level airport with a 1,500 ft HAA, has a Category C radius of 2.86 NM, 1.16 NM (68.5%) larger than before. The extra room lets pilots maneuver instead of using the high descent rates the old small areas often forced [[29:149|IPH 4-9]].

bullets: Protection exists only at or above the MDA and inside the area. Below the MDA the pilot must see and avoid obstacles [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]].
A restriction note can close part of the area, such as "Circling NA E of RWY 17-35" [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]].
Leaving the area at the MDA, even onto the missed approach track, may not keep vertical obstacle clearance; extra climb inside the area may be needed first [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]].

callout.text: The IPH drawing of the circling area (Figure 4-2) lists only the old standard radii, and the IFH drawing (Figure 10-12) shows radii that vary with category alone [[29:149|IPH 4-9]] [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]. Teach from the AIM table and have the learner check every chart for the C symbol [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]].

check.q: The circling line has no C symbol and your learner flies Category B. How far from the runway ends is she protected?
check.a: 1.5 NM, the standard Category B radius at all altitudes [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]]; no C symbol means the standard area [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]].

body.p: **Circling approach minimums on the selected instrument approach chart.** Circling minimums are the MDA and visibility required for the circle-to-land maneuver, listed under each category [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]]. The MDA is in feet MSL and is also given as HAA, the height above airport elevation; figures in parentheses are military and not used in civil aviation [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]]. With no dividing line between categories, one set of minimums covers two or more of them, and a visibility in statute miles follows a hyphen, as in 530-1 [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]].
In the Chart Users' Guide example the airport elevation is 1179 and the circling line reads 1540-1 (HAA 361) for A, 1640-1 for B, 1640-1½ for C and 1740-2 for D [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]].

**A real chart: Charlotte ILS or LOC RWY 18L** (IPH Figure 4-45, a 2017 chart; brief only current charts). The C symbol sits beside CIRCLING, so the expanded radii apply [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]]. Circling is 1320-1 (HAA 572) for A and B, 1500-2¼ for C and 1500-2½ for D; a second set, ZIMOG fix minimums (DME required), gives 1240-1 for A and B. The notes say "Circling NA at night" [[29:214|IPH Figure 4-45]].

bullets: Two sets of minimums: one for the pilot who can identify a stepdown fix and one for the pilot who cannot, or for a second altimeter source [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20e]].
Remote altimeter notes can raise MDAs, for example "use SLN altimeter setting and increase all MDAs 40 feet" [[2:103|Chart Users' Guide p 103]].
The authorized MDA is the highest of the procedure's MDA, the one prescribed for the pilot in command, and the one for the equipment available and used [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]].
On an RNAV (GPS) chart the circling MDA may be lower than the LNAV/VNAV DA but never lower than the LNAV MDA [[33:411|AIM 5-4-5f]].
Circling-only charts show no TDZE [[2:122|Chart Users' Guide p 122]]; the top strip shows N/A for runway landing distance and TDZE [[2:102|Chart Users' Guide p 102]].
Cold weather: in the IFH temperature-correction example, a 1,000 ft circling MDA becomes 1,200 ft at -50 °C [[23:101|IFH 5-6]].

callout.text: Application: have the learner read the circling line aloud in the same order every time: category and speed, MDA, HAA, visibility, symbol, notes. Then ask what changes if the speed goes up 10 knots.

check.q: On the Charlotte chart your Category A learner has DME and identifies ZIMOG. Which circling MDA and visibility apply?
check.a: 1240-1, HAA 492, from the ZIMOG fix minimums [[29:214|IPH Figure 4-45]]; two sets are published for pilots who can and cannot identify the fix [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20e]].

body.p: **Compliance with advisories, clearance instructions, and/or restrictions.** Teach each source of "where and how you may circle" by name, so the learner knows it before the MDA.

What the learner does
rows: Restriction note on the chart
No circling in the restricted part; the note may apply to some categories only and may differ by day and night [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f1]]
Night circling NA
Published when obstacles penetrating the visual surface are not marked and lighted [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]

Follow the controller's instructions; a clearance does not cancel a published circling restriction [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f2]]
"Circle to Runway Two Two"
The runway in use is not the one the approach serves; ATC may add a direction and a leg, as in "circle northwest of the airport for a right downwind" [[34:324|AIM P/CG Circle to runway]]
No landing runway in the clearance
The pilot may land on any runway [[29:136|IPH 3-24]]
Non-towered airport

Use the turn direction of 14 CFR 91.126(b) unless a restriction requires the opposite; overflying the airport to see the wind and turn indicators may help [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f3]]. In Class G that means left turns unless approved lights or markings show right turns [[60:451|14 CFR 91.126(b)]]

The rule to circle the airport to the left does not apply to a circling approach under part 97 [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(f)]]

Give the controller the approach category; the controller then gives the MDA [[33:431|AIM 5-4-11c2]]

body.p: Asheville's radar minimums put a restriction in words: "Circling not authorized west of Rwy 16-34. Night circling not authorized." Category A circles at 3000-1 and Category D at 3000-2¾, all with an HAA of 835 [[29:226|IPH Figure 4-56]].

bullets: Circling is prohibited from a GLS, from an ILS without a localizer line of minima, and from an RNAV (GPS) approach without an LNAV line [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f5]].
In some busy terminal areas ATC may not allow circling, and no circling minimums are published [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20f]].

callout.text: Remain vigilant for other traffic while circling [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f4]]. In the midair studies the AIH cites, the vast majority of collisions happened at or near nontowered airports below 1,000 ft [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Application: a circle at a non-towered field is flown in exactly that airspace, so the instructor's eyes stay outside.

check.q: The tower says "circle west of the airport for a left downwind Runway 34," but the chart says circling is not authorized west of Rwy 16-34. What does your learner do?
check.a: Stay out of the restricted area and tell the controller: an ATC clearance does not negate a published circling restriction [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f2]] [[29:226|IPH Figure 4-56]].

chunks.title: Choosing the maneuver for the airplane and the day

body.p: **Selection of the appropriate circling approach maneuver considering the maneuvering capabilities of the aircraft.** The IFH bases the choice on personal flying capability and knowledge of the airplane's performance, and lists the factors: airport design, ceiling and visibility, wind direction and velocity, final approach course alignment, distance from the FAF to the runway, and ATC instructions [[23:311|IFH 10-20]] [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]. The AIM says the same: sound judgment and knowledge of the pilot's and the airplane's capabilities decide the exact maneuver, since airport design and the airplane's position, altitude and airspeed must all be considered [[34:3|AIM 5-5-4a2(g)]] [[34:4|AIM 5-5-4a2(g)]].

head: Pattern
When the IFH uses it
rows: A
Final course crosses the runway centerline at less than 90°, and the runway is in sight early enough for a base leg [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]
B
Runway seen too late for pattern A: circle the runway [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]
C
Landing opposite the final course, with the runway sighted in time to turn downwind [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]
D
Runway sighted too late for a turn to downwind; the IFH drawing crosses over the runway and loops back to land [[23:311|IFH 10-20]] [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]

body.p: **What the airplane's capability changes.** The AIM lists four factors that shape the ground track when maneuvering above the category speed; they are worth teaching for every circle [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7c]] [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c]]:

bullets: Bank angle: at 165 knots groundspeed the turn radius is 4,194 ft at 30° of bank but 6,654 ft at 20°. With a shallow bank the path or speed may need to change to stay inside the area; excessive bank can lead to loss of control [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7c1]] [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c1]].
Indicated airspeed: the design uses the highest speed of the category; fly faster and something else must change [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c2]].
Wind: on downwind the groundspeed can be much higher than the indicated airspeed, so plan the start of every turn [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c3]].
Technique: plan the lateral and vertical path with current weather and terrain information [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c4]].
Base or downwind: choose from the weather, VFR traffic, the altitude to lose at normal descent rates, and any restriction [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f4]].
Circle higher when you can: if the ceiling allows, fly nearer VFR pattern altitude for safer maneuvering and a more normal view of the runway [[23:311|IFH 10-20]].

body.p: A procedure aligned with a runway may still be circling-only because the descent gradient is too steep. A VDA on it does not mean a straight-in landing is recommended or even possible; the descent rate may exceed the airplane's capability, and the pilot must decide how best to maneuver within the circling area [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k4]] [[33:415|AIM 5-4-5k4]].

callout.text: Application: in a slow trainer, teach the tightest pattern that keeps the runway in view and still allows a normal descent. In a faster airplane the same pattern may not fit, and the learner must know that before reaching the MDA.

check.q: The final course is aligned with Runway 18, the wind favors Runway 36, and the runway appears in time to turn downwind. Which IFH pattern fits?
check.a: Pattern C: landing opposite the direction of the final approach, with the runway sighted in time for a turn to the downwind leg [[23:311|IFH 10-20]].

chunks.title: A pattern that fits the visibility and the radius

body.p: **Importance of flying a circling approach pattern that does not exceed the published visibility criteria.** Three rules tie the size of the pattern to the visibility:

bullets: At or above the MDA in the circle, an identifiable part of the airport must stay distinctly visible; if not, a missed approach at once, unless only a normal bank hides it [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]].
To go below the MDA the flight visibility must be at least the visibility in the procedure [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(2)]], and no landing with less [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(d)(2)]].
Remain within the radius for the category and the MDA [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f4]].

body.p: Published visibility depends on the HAA for circling approaches, the approach lights and the type of procedure [[29:179|IPH 4-39]], and the circling area grows with category [[29:148|IPH 4-8]]. At Charlotte, Categories A and B need 1 mile, C needs 2¼ and D 2½ [[29:214|IPH Figure 4-45]].

Do the arithmetic with the learner. There are 5,280 ft in a statute mile and 6,076.1 ft in a nautical mile [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]], so 1 SM is about 0.87 NM, while the standard Category A radius is 1.3 NM [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]]. With exactly 1 mile of flight visibility, a pattern flown out near the edge of the area can put the airport beyond sight, and then the circle must end in a missed approach [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]].

callout.text: Application: teach the radius as an outer fence, not a target. Fly close enough to keep an identifiable part of the airport in view and to make a normal descent, and start turns early when a tailwind on downwind pushes the airplane out [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c3]].

body.p: The IFH technique is to keep visual contact with the runway of intended landing during the circle [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]. An EFVS does not replace the eyes here: it cannot satisfy the requirement to see an identifiable part of the airport during the circle at or above the MDA or while descending from it [[29:161|IPH 4-21]].

check.q: In 1¼ miles of visibility your learner flies a wide downwind and loses sight of the airport, but says he is still inside the 1.5 NM radius. Is that acceptable?
check.a: No. Staying inside the radius is not enough: when an identifiable part of the airport is not distinctly visible during the circle, a missed approach is required at once [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]].

chunks.title: Holding the MDA until in position to land

body.p: **Maintenance of an altitude no lower than the circling MDA until in a position from which a descent to a normal landing can be made.**

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.175(c): no operation below the authorized MDA unless (1) the aircraft is continuously in a position from which a descent to a landing on the intended runway can be made at a normal rate of descent using normal maneuvers, (2) the flight visibility is not less than the visibility in the procedure, and (3) at least one listed visual reference for the intended runway is distinctly visible and identifiable [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(c)]] [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]].

body.p: The AIM and the IPH apply it to the circle: remain at or above the circling altitude until continuously in that position [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20f]] [[29:149|IPH 4-9]]. Seeing the runway is not the trigger; being in position is.

bullets: Application: being in position should let a stabilized descent follow. The IPH stabilized approach concept is a constant approach speed, descent rate, vertical flight path and configuration, and it is strongly recommended for propeller-driven airplanes [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].
A descent rate over about 1,000 fpm below 1,000 ft AGL is unacceptable [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].
The IPH turbojet standard for the final segment of a circle: stabilized by 500 ft above airport elevation or at the MDA, whichever is lower [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].
Below the MDA there is no charted obstacle protection; the pilot must see and avoid [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]].

body.p: **Holding the MDA while looking outside.** A single pilot must keep flying by the instruments while acquiring the runway, which is harder than in a two-pilot crew [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]. With an altitude preselector, set the MDA so the airplane cannot descend below it, rounding up when the selector moves in 100 ft steps: the IPH sets 700 for a 660 ft MDA [[29:176|IPH 4-36]]. Once level, set the missed approach altitude, because accurate flight director guidance is not available for a missed approach if the MDA is left set [[29:176|IPH 4-36]] [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

callout.text: Not "runway in sight, start down." Say: "In position, normal rate, normal maneuvers, visibility, reference: leaving the MDA" [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]].

check.q: Abeam the threshold on downwind at the MDA, your learner pulls the power to "get down while it's close." What do you say?
check.a: Not yet: he may leave the MDA only when continuously in a position to descend to the runway at a normal rate using normal maneuvers [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]]. Have him fly the pattern to where a stabilized, normal-rate descent fits [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

chunks.title: Losing sight of the airport: the circling missed approach

callout.text: Missed approach immediately whenever an identifiable part of the airport is not distinctly visible during a circling maneuver at or above the MDA, unless only a normal bank of the aircraft hides it [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]; and below the MDA whenever the 91.175(c) requirements are not met [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]].

body.p: If visual reference is lost while circling, follow the missed approach for that procedure unless ATC gives another. Make an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway and keep turning until established on the missed approach course. The pattern depends on where the airplane was when sight was lost, and following the procedure keeps it laterally within the circling and missed approach obstruction clearance areas [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]] [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21c]].

bullets: A missed approach after starting to maneuver usually begins beyond the MAP [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]].

From a circle, the published missed approach does not necessarily give obstacle clearance or traffic separation [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]]; extra climb inside the circling area may be needed before joining the missed approach track [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]].

Different case: still on the final course before the circle starts, a pilot who goes missed early flies the procedure to the MAP at or above the MDA before turning, unless ATC clears otherwise [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]].

Fly the go-around: climb pitch while setting climb power, configure for climb, turn, tell ATC and request further clearance [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]. Power first, then attitude, then configuration, with flaps up in small steps [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Climb to a safe altitude before leaving the published missed approach [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21g]].

body.p: Plan it before the approach: assess the actions for a balked landing beyond the MAP or below the MDA, with the expected weather and the airplane's performance [[29:180|IPH 4-40]]. The missed approach comes when workload is at its maximum, so study and master it before beginning the approach [[23:312|IFH 10-21]].

callout.text: Re-entering cloud while circling is an inadvertent IMC encounter: commit to the instruments at once, because searching outside for visual references can lead to spatial disorientation and complete loss of control [[29:290|IPH A-4]].

check.q: Your learner loses sight of the airport on a left downwind for the landing runway. Which way does he turn, and until when?
check.a: Left: an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway, continued until established on the missed approach course [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]] [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21c]].

chunks.title: Risk: night, illusions and the low turn to final

bullets: Illusions: featureless terrain such as water, dark areas or snow, and rain on the windscreen, create an illusion of greater height; haze makes the runway seem farther away; all lead to a lower approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5a3(d)]] [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5a3(e)]].
Bright runway lights with few lights around make the runway seem closer, leading to a higher approach; lights along a road can be mistaken for runway lights [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5a3(f)]].

Defenses: expect illusions at unfamiliar airports, especially at night or in bad weather; check the altimeter often; look the airport over from the air if possible; use VASI, PAPI or an electronic glideslope [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

Low visibility: finding a strange runway quickly is hard, especially circling to an airport with few lights or one inside distracting city lights; know the approach lights before starting [[23:281|IFH 9-38]].

body.p: **The turn to final.** A tailwind on base can make the pilot turn late and overshoot. Steepening the bank with back pressure and inside rudder sets up a skidding cross-control stall that can quickly become a spin. The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around; at that height be reluctant to bank past 30° and never skid the turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Stalling speed rises in proportion to the square root of the load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

Distraction is the trap: most stall/spin accidents came when attention was diverted, and 60 percent happened during takeoff and landing [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Application: in a circle the configuration change, the traffic watch, the runway search and the altimeter all compete for the same minute.

callout.text: Go-arounds get delayed by landing expectancy and pride. A go-around is not dangerous in itself; it becomes dangerous only when delayed or done wrong [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

check.q: Night circle to a runway with dark water on three sides. Which way will your learner tend to err, and what do you teach?
check.a: Low: featureless terrain creates an illusion of greater height, so pilots fly a lower approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5a3(d)]]. Teach frequent altimeter checks and the use of VASI or PAPI when available [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

body.p: **Exhibits instructional knowledge of common errors related to a circling approach.** The PTS says the listed errors may or may not appear in the references; they are listed because they happen often (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). For each one, say what you see, the usual cause and the fix.

**Failure to have essential knowledge of the circling approach information on the instrument approach chart (K2a).** **Failure to adhere to the published MDA and visibility criteria during the circling approach maneuver (K2b).** **Inappropriate pilot technique during transition from the circling maneuver to the landing approach (K2c).**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how you teach it
rows: K2a: wrong category line
Briefs the A line, then circles at 100 knots
Category taken from the airplane, not the speed
Brief speed and category together; faster means the higher line [[29:148|IPH 4-8]] [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]]
K2a: radius unknown
Cannot say how far out the protection goes; flies a big pattern
Never checked for the C symbol
Read the symbol and the AIM table in every briefing [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]] [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]]
K2a: notes missed
Plans to circle on the restricted side, or at night where NA
Briefing skipped the notes
Brief the notes before the IAF; restrictions bind even under a clearance [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f1]] [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f2]]
K2b: early descent
Below the MDA as soon as the runway shows on downwind
Landing expectancy [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; "in sight" taken as "in position"
Hold the MDA until 91.175(c) is met [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]]; MDA in the preselector [[29:176|IPH 4-36]]
K2b: altitude sag
MDA drifts low while the learner looks outside
Single-pilot scan stops during the runway search [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]
Short looks outside with the altimeter in every pass; the MDA is a floor [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20f]]
K2b: pattern beyond the visibility
Wide downwind, airport fades, learner keeps going
No plan for the tailwind; radius treated as a target
Plan turns for the groundspeed [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c3]]; airport not distinctly visible means missed approach [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]
K2c: overshoot fixed with bank and rudder
Late turn to final, bank steepening, ball off center
Tailwind on base, late turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Go around; be reluctant to bank past 30° that low, and never skid the turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
K2c: dive from the MDA
VSI past 1,000 fpm on a short final
Left the MDA too late or too close in
Over about 1,000 fpm below 1,000 ft AGL is unacceptable [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]; unstabilized means go around [[29:180|IPH 4-40]]
K2c: late configuration
Full flaps in one step on short final; pitch and speed swing
Configuring after the descent starts
Limit low-altitude configuration changes [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]; flaps in increments support a stabilized approach [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]
K2c: illusion
Low approach over dark terrain or in rain
Featureless terrain or rain on the windscreen [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5a3(d)]]
Altimeter checks and VASI or PAPI [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]

body.p: Analyze before you correct: when the learner thinks aloud you can tell a misconception from a lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Your learner briefs the circling line perfectly but cannot say whether the C symbol is on it. Which error is this, and why does it matter?
check.a: Failure to have essential knowledge of the circling information on the chart (K2a). Without the symbol he cannot know whether the standard or the expanded radius protects him [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]] [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]].

chunks.title: Teaching it safely: ground, simulator, altitude, airport

body.p: Build the circle in layers. The AIH's integrated method: knowledge on the ground, procedure practice in a simulator until proficient, then the airplane to verify proficiency [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

head: Stage
What you do
rows: Ground

Category and speed, the circling line and notes, the radius and symbol, the missed approach from the circle [[29:149|IPH 4-9]] [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]; objectives, completion standards and safety procedures [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]
Simulator
Practice the chart work, the patterns and the lost-sight turn; the FAA recommends training in the simulator until the tasks are done successfully before trying them in the airplane [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]
At altitude
IFH circling approach patterns I and II on an imaginary runway: timed legs, standard-rate turns, gear and flaps, a 500 fpm descent for 500 ft, then a constant-airspeed climb [[23:193|IFH 7-32]]
Real airport, good VMC

View-limiting device on to the MDA and off for the visual circle; the device does not apply to elements that need visual references, and you brief when and how it comes off (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction)
Marginal weather
Only within limits briefed on the ground; personal minimums are set more restrictive than the regulations [[30:13|RMH 2-1]]

bullets: Brief the positive three-step exchange of flight controls before flight [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Be ready to take control at any time with hazardous maneuvers, especially on a learner's first attempts [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]; a learner should never be allowed to exceed your limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

Letting a learner go part of the way into a mistake helps learning only when safety permits [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Application: in the circle that never includes going below the MDA, leaving the area or skidding the turn to final.
Talking point for personal minimums: many Part 121 and 135 operators may not circle below a 1,000 ft MDA and 3 SM visibility [[29:160|IPH 4-20]].

check.q: Why fly IFH circling pattern I at altitude before the learner's first real circle?
check.a: It drills timed legs, standard-rate turns, the gear and flap change and a 500 fpm descent and climb on an imaginary runway with height to spare [[23:193|IFH 7-32]], so the workload is met before it happens near the ground.

body.p: **Demonstrates and simultaneously explains a circling approach from an instructional standpoint.** In "instructor tells, instructor does," explain power settings, attitudes and other factors as you fly, in the same order as the briefing; if the demonstration strays from the explanation, acknowledge and explain it at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. The explanation must be clear, concise, technically accurate and complete with no prompting (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). You must also fly it to the INSTRUMENT PILOT skill level while instructing (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction); lesson IR.VI.D gives the Instrument ACS tolerances for the circle: airspeed ±10 knots, heading or track ±10° and altitude +100/-0 ft until leaving the MDA or the chosen circling altitude (ACS IR.VI.D.S5).
**A talk-through you can use** (put in your POH speeds; this one is for a trainer flown at 90 knots):

bullets: Before the IAF: "Ninety knots is Category A. Circling line for A; the C symbol is (or is not) there, so our radius is __ NM. Notes: any restriction or night NA? If I lose the airport: climbing turn toward the landing runway, then the missed approach" [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]] [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]] [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]].

On final: "MDA set in the preselector. I plan to be level at the MDA well before the MAP, which the circle shares with the straight-in nonprecision approach" [[29:176|IPH 4-36]] [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f5]].
At the MDA: "Level, missed approach altitude set. Airport in sight, landing Runway __, pattern C to a left downwind, staying inside the radius" [[29:177|IPH 4-37]] [[23:311|IFH 10-20]].
On downwind: "Holding the MDA. Tailwind, so the groundspeed is high and I turn base early. I am not yet in position for a normal descent" [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c3]] [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]].

Turning base: "Now in position: normal rate, normal maneuvers, visibility and runway in sight. Leaving the MDA, stabilized, no more than 30° of bank, no skid" [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

If sight is lost: "Airport not in sight: power, climb attitude, climbing turn toward the runway, flaps up in steps, missed approach" [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]] [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

body.p: Then reverse the roles: in "learner tells, instructor does" the learner talks you through the circle, so misunderstandings surface before he is busy flying; in "learner tells, learner does" he flies and thinks aloud [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: Positive exchange: "You have the flight controls." "I have the flight controls." "You have the flight controls." Add a visual check [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: During your demonstration you sink 60 ft below the circling MDA while pointing out the runway. What do you do?
check.a: Correct it and say so right away: when a demonstration does not match the explanation, acknowledge and explain the deviation at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. The MDA is a floor until in position for a normal descent [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]].

chunks.title: Checkride: analyze and correct simulated errors

body.p: **Analyzes and corrects simulated common errors related to a circling approach.** During selected maneuvers the evaluator acts as your student, and will not simulate any condition that could jeopardize safe flight (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). Name the error, say what you see, explain the cause, give the fix, and say how you would teach it.

head: The examiner does
You name it and fix it
rows: Circles a Category A airplane at 100 knots on the A line
Wrong category: 100 knots is Category B speed [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]; brief speed and category in preflight [[29:149|IPH 4-9]]
Starts down on downwind the moment the runway appears
Early descent below the MDA; hold it until in position for a normal descent [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]]
Extends downwind in a tailwind until the airport fades
Pattern beyond the visibility: missed approach required [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]; plan turns for the groundspeed [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c3]]
Calls "lost the airport" and turns straight to the missed approach course
Wrong turn: climbing turn toward the landing runway first [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]]
Overshoots final and feeds in bottom rudder
Skidding turn near the ground: go around [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Turns into a restricted area because the tower said to
A clearance does not negate a published restriction [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f2]]

body.p: To check real understanding, have the learner vary the circle or combine it with another task, such as a different landing runway or a missed approach; a learner who only memorized will struggle [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: Application: you are still responsible for safe flight. If a simulated error carries the airplane below the MDA near obstacles or into a skid near the ground, take the controls with "I have the flight controls" [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Any action or lack of action that requires the evaluator to intervene for safety is a typical reason for an unsatisfactory (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

check.q: The examiner, as your learner, loses sight of the airport on the far side of the circle and rolls toward the published missed approach course, away from the field. What do you say?
check.a: Name it: wrong missed approach from a circle. Make an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway and continue until established on the missed approach course, which keeps the airplane in the protected areas [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]] [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21c]].

scenario.title: A radar approach and a circle at Asheville
scenario.setup: You are a CFII. Your instrument learner, a few lessons from his checkride, flies a fixed-gear trainer with no published VREF; 1.3 VSO is 78 knots, so it is Category A. Today's lesson uses the Asheville radar minimums in IPH Figure 4-56 as the chart: an ASR approach to Runway 34, then a circle to land on Runway 16, which the gusty wind favors. The weather is good VMC. The learner flies under a view-limiting device to the MDA, and you simulate a 1,100 ft overcast and 2 miles of visibility in mist. You are instructor and safety pilot, and the flight ends near sunset.

questions.q: On the ground the learner plans to fly the circle at 95 knots because of the gusts. Which circling line does he brief?
questions.a: 95 knots is a Category B speed [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]], so he briefs the B line: 3000-1¼, HAA 835 [[29:226|IPH Figure 4-56]]. Faster than the category means the higher category's minimums [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]], which keeps the airplane in the larger area built for that speed [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

questions.q: Before the descent, the controller asks for the aircraft approach category. Why, and what does he answer?
questions.a: When a surveillance approach will end in a circle-to-land, the pilot must give the category, and the controller then gives the MDA [[33:431|AIM 5-4-11c2]]. He answers Category B, the category for the speed he will fly [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]].

questions.q: Level at 3000 ft, you lift the device. The learner sees the runway and starts a left turn to the west to set up for Runway 16. What do you say?
questions.a: The chart note says circling is not authorized west of Rwy 16-34 [[29:226|IPH Figure 4-56]]; no circling maneuvers in a restricted area, and a tower clearance would not cancel it [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f1]] [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f2]]. Circle on the east side; landing opposite the final course with the runway in sight in time for a downwind is IFH pattern C [[23:311|IFH 10-20]].

questions.q: On the east downwind, abeam the threshold, he reduces power because "the runway is right there." What do you teach?
questions.a: Stay at the MDA until continuously in a position to descend at a normal rate using normal maneuvers [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]]. There are 835 ft to lose [[29:226|IPH Figure 4-56]], and a descent over about 1,000 fpm below 1,000 ft AGL is unacceptable [[29:177|IPH 4-37]], so the descent has to fit the pattern, not the other way around.

questions.q: On base you tell him the mist has swallowed the airport. What does he do?
questions.a: Missed approach at once, since no identifiable part of the airport is distinctly visible [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]: an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway, continued until established on the missed approach course [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]]. From a circle the published missed approach does not necessarily give obstacle clearance, so extra climb inside the circling area may be needed before joining the track [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]] [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]].

questions.q: The sun is setting as you set up for another try, and the wind still favors Runway 16. Can he circle again?
questions.a: Not at night: the note says night circling is not authorized [[29:226|IPH Figure 4-56]]. Such notes are published when obstacles penetrating the visual surface are not marked and lighted [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]. In the debrief, use collaborative assessment: his self-assessment first, then yours [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

skills.do: Fly a nonprecision approach to the circling MDA and a circle to land while explaining the category for the speed flown, the circling line and notes, the radius, when you will leave the MDA, the turn to final and the missed approach from the circle.
skills.practice: Fly IFH circling patterns I and II at altitude [[23:193|IFH 7-32]], then talk through real circles in a simulator and in good VMC, explaining in the same order you fly [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

skills.do: As the examiner flies the errors (wrong category line, early descent, a pattern beyond the visibility, the wrong missed approach turn, a skidding turn to final), name each one, explain its cause, give the fix and say how you would teach it.
skills.practice: Learn the error table with a "what you see" for each row, and take turns flying the errors with another applicant at a safe altitude or in a simulator; the evaluator will not simulate anything that could jeopardize safe flight (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). Analyze before correcting [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

quiz.q: Your learner's airplane has no published VREF and a VSO of 60 knots. He plans to circle at 100 knots in gusty wind. Which circling line does he use?
options: Category A, since 1.3 VSO is 78 knots
Category B, for the 100 knots he will fly
Category C, one category above his speed
Category A, raised 100 ft to allow for the gusts
quiz.why: 1.3 x 60 = 78 knots makes the airplane Category A [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]], but faster than the category's top speed means the higher category's minimums, and 100 knots is a Category B speed [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]] [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]. Raising the A line is not a method the sources give.

quiz.q: How can your learner tell from the chart that the expanded circling radii apply?
options: The word EXPANDED printed in the chart's notes box
The letter E after the circling visibility
A shaded ring drawn around the airport in the plan view
A white C in a black square on the circling line
quiz.why: Expanded areas are identified by the "negative C" symbol on the circling line; its absence means the standard radii [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]] [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]].

quiz.q: At Charlotte the circling line has the C symbol. Your Category C learner circles at the 1500 ft MDA. What radius protects him?
options: 1.7 NM
2.7 NM
2.8 NM
3.7 NM
quiz.why: 1500 ft is in the 1001-3000 ft row of the expanded table, where Category C is 2.8 NM [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]] [[29:214|IPH Figure 4-45]]. 1.7 NM is the standard Category C radius, which applies only without the C symbol; 2.7 NM is for MDAs of 1,000 ft or less.

quiz.q: On downwind at the circling MDA the runway is in plain view. When may your learner start down?
options: As soon as the runway is distinctly visible
When abeam the landing threshold on downwind
When in position for a normal descent and landing
When the tower reports visibility at minimums
quiz.why: No descent below the MDA until continuously in a position to descend to the runway at a normal rate using normal maneuvers, with the visibility and a visual reference also required [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]] [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20f]]. Seeing the runway is only one of the conditions.

quiz.q: Your learner loses sight of the airport on a right downwind in the circle. What is his first move?
options: A climbing right turn toward the landing runway
A straight climb ahead on the downwind heading
A turn directly onto the missed approach course
A slight descent to get below the cloud and look
quiz.why: If visual reference is lost while circling, make an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway and continue until established on the missed approach course [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]]; that keeps the airplane inside the circling and missed approach clearance areas [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21c]]. Turning straight to the course can leave them.

quiz.q: The tower clears your learner to circle through an area a chart note says is Circling NA. What do you teach?
options: The clearance overrides the note, so follow the tower
Obey the note and tell the controller he is unable
Follow the tower but stay 500 ft above the MDA
Ignore the note by day; it binds only at night
quiz.why: At towered airports follow the controller during the circle, but an ATC clearance does not negate published circling area restrictions [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f2]]. Restrictions may differ between day and night, so read the note as written [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f1]].

quiz.q: At a non-towered Class G airport with no restriction and no right-traffic markings, which way are the turns in the circle?
options: Left turns, per 91.126(b)
Right turns, away from the final course
Either way the pilot prefers to fly
Toward the missed approach course
quiz.why: At non-towered airports use the turn direction of 91.126(b) unless a restriction requires the opposite [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f3]]; in Class G that means all turns to the left unless approved light signals or markings show right turns [[60:451|14 CFR 91.126(b)]].

quiz.q: How much obstacle clearance do published circling minimums provide, and where?
options: 250 ft, along the final course only
500 ft, within 5 NM of the airport
1,000 ft, anywhere the runway is seen
300 ft, inside the circling area
quiz.why: Circling minimums provide a minimum of 300 ft of obstacle clearance in the circling area [[23:311|IFH 10-20]] [[29:149|IPH 4-9]], and only while the pilot stays within that area [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20f]].

quiz.q: Your learner's RNAV (GPS) chart shows only LPV and LNAV/VNAV lines, and the wind requires a circle. Can he circle from it?
options: Yes, at the LNAV/VNAV DA plus 100 ft
Yes, at the LPV DA with 1 mile visibility
No, circling needs an LNAV line of minima
Yes, if ATC approves the circle to land on request
quiz.why: Circling from an RNAV (GPS) approach without an LNAV line of minima is prohibited, as is circling from a GLS or from an ILS without a localizer line [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f5]].

quiz.q: What does the HAA printed under a circling MDA tell your learner?
options: Height of the MDA above the touchdown zone
Height of the MDA above the published airport elevation
Height of the MDA above the highest obstacle
Height of the airplane above the terrain
quiz.why: HAA is the height of the MDA above the published airport elevation, published with circling minimums [[34:356|AIM P/CG Height above airport]]. Height above the touchdown zone (HAT) goes with straight-in minimums [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]].

quiz.q: The final course crosses the runway centerline at 60°, and the runway is in sight early enough for a base leg. Which IFH pattern fits?
options: Pattern A
Pattern B
Pattern C
Pattern D
quiz.why: Pattern A can be flown when the final approach course intersects the runway centerline at less than 90° and the runway is in sight early enough to establish a base leg; B is for a runway seen too late for A [[23:311|IFH 10-20]].

quiz.q: Leaving the MDA late on a short final, your learner's VSI shows 1,300 fpm at 400 ft AGL. What does the IPH say?
options: Acceptable if the touchdown is still in the first third
Acceptable in propeller airplanes below 500 ft
Unacceptable, but only in turbojet airplanes
Unacceptable: over about 1,000 fpm below 1,000 ft
quiz.why: A descent rate greater than about 1,000 fpm is unacceptable in the final stages of an approach, below 1,000 ft AGL, because of a human perceptual limit independent of airplane type [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]; an approach that becomes unstabilized calls for a missed approach [[29:180|IPH 4-40]].

final_quiz.q: On the Charlotte chart your Category A learner has DME and identifies ZIMOG. What are his circling minimums?
final_quiz.why: With ZIMOG identified (DME required), the ZIMOG fix minimums apply: circling 1240-1, HAA 492, for A and B [[29:214|IPH Figure 4-45]]. Two sets are published for pilots who can and cannot identify a fix [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20e]]. 1320-1 is the line without ZIMOG, and 1140/55 is the S-LOC line.

final_quiz.q: A night arrival at Charlotte needs a circle to land. What does the chart tell your learner?
options: Circling NA at night; plan a straight-in
Circle at night using the Category D line
Circle only with the ZIMOG fix identified
Circle only in a right-hand pattern at night
final_quiz.why: The notes say "Circling NA at night" [[29:214|IPH Figure 4-45]]. Such notes are published when obstacles penetrating the visual surface are not marked and lighted [[29:179|IPH 4-39]].

final_quiz.q: No higher-category line is published, but your learner must circle above his category's top speed. Which factors does the AIM say to weigh?
options: Only the reported ceiling and the visibility at the field
The HAA, the TDZE and the runway length
Bank, indicated airspeed, wind and technique
Weight and balance and density altitude
final_quiz.why: A pilot using an alternative method should consider bank angle, indicated airspeed, wind speed and direction, and pilot technique, because they change the ground track and the containment in the protected area [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7c]] [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies the circle with 20° of bank to be gentle with the passengers. What does the AIM warn?
options: Any bank under 30° keeps the turn inside the area
Banks under 25° are not allowed below the MDA
A shallow bank raises the stall speed sharply
A shallow bank widens the turn and can leave the area
final_quiz.why: At 165 knots groundspeed the turn radius grows from 4,194 ft at 30° to 6,654 ft at 20°; with a shallow bank the path or speed may need to change to stay inside, while excessive bank can lead to loss of control [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7c1]] [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c1]]. Stall speed rises with load factor, so a steeper bank, not a shallower one, raises it [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

final_quiz.q: After losing the airport in the circle, your learner flies the published missed approach. Is obstacle clearance assured?
options: Yes, a missed approach is always protected
Yes, once he reaches the missed approach holding fix
No, extra climb inside the area may be needed
No, so he should descend to find the runway
final_quiz.why: From a circle the published missed approach does not necessarily give obstacle clearance or traffic separation [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]]. Joining the missed approach track may not give vertical clearance once outside the circling area, so more climb inside it may be needed [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]].

final_quiz.q: In a normal bank on the turn to base, the wing hides the airport for a moment. What does 91.175(e)(2) require?
options: An immediate missed approach
Nothing, if only the bank hid it
A report to ATC that visual contact was lost
A climb of at least 300 ft above the MDA
final_quiz.why: A missed approach is required when an identifiable part of the airport is not distinctly visible during a circling maneuver at or above the MDA, unless the inability to see it results only from a normal bank during the circle [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: Still on the final course and short of the MAP, before starting to circle, your learner decides to go missed. What does the AIM say?
options: Fly to the MAP at or above the MDA, then turn
Turn at once toward the landing runway and climb
Climb straight ahead to the MSA, then turn
Turn to the missed approach fix right away
final_quiz.why: No consideration is given to an abnormally early turn: on an early missed approach, unless ATC clears otherwise, fly the procedure to the MAP at or above the MDA before turning [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. The climbing turn toward the runway is for a pilot who loses visual reference while circling [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]].

final_quiz.q: Your corporate learner's airplane has an EFVS. Can its image keep the circle going when the airport is not visible to the eye?
options: Yes, EFVS may replace natural vision in the circle
Yes, but only while at or above the circling MDA
Yes, if the enhanced visibility meets the minimum
No, the references must be seen with natural vision
final_quiz.why: EFVS is not intended as a sufficient visual system for circling; it may be used only if the required references stay distinctly visible with natural vision, and it cannot satisfy the requirement that an identifiable part of the airport be distinctly visible during the circle [[29:161|IPH 4-21]].

final_quiz.q: An ASR approach will end in a circle to land. What must your learner tell the controller?
options: The circling pattern he plans to fly
The intended touchdown point
The runway visual range he sees
The aircraft approach category
final_quiz.why: When a surveillance approach will terminate in a circle-to-land maneuver, the pilot must furnish the aircraft approach category, and the controller then provides the MDA [[33:431|AIM 5-4-11c2]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner wants to land opposite the final course but sights the runway too late to turn downwind. Which IFH pattern?
options: Pattern A
Pattern B
Pattern C
Pattern D
final_quiz.why: If the runway is sighted too late for a turn to downwind, fly pattern D; pattern C is for a runway sighted in time for the downwind [[23:311|IFH 10-20]].

final_quiz.q: Circling at night to a runway with dark water on three sides, how will your learner tend to fly the visual descent?
options: Too low, from an illusion of greater height
Too high, from an illusion of being close
Too fast, from an illusion of a slow descent
Too wide, from an illusion of a narrow runway
final_quiz.why: Featureless terrain such as water or darkened areas creates the illusion of being higher than one is, so the pilot flies a lower approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5a3(d)]]. Bright runway lights with dark surroundings are the case that leads to a higher approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5a3(f)]].

final_quiz.q: Before your learner's first real circle, what does the IFH give you to practice the workload at a safe height?
options: Circling patterns flown to an imaginary runway
Steep spirals around a point at the circling MDA
Timed turns to headings under the hood only
Partial panel stalls in landing configuration
final_quiz.why: The IFH gives circling approach patterns I and II on an imaginary runway: timed legs, standard-rate turns, gear and flaps, a 500 fpm descent for 500 ft and a climb [[23:193|IFH 7-32]]. The AIH adds simulator practice before the airplane [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

final_quiz.q: On the checkride you sink 70 ft below the circling MDA while explaining the pattern. What should you do?
options: Say nothing; the examiner may miss it
Correct it and say so at once
Keep descending; the runway is in sight
Call it a planned error for him to find
final_quiz.why: If a demonstration does not conform to the explanation, acknowledge and explain the deviation immediately [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. The MDA is a floor until the airplane is in position for a normal descent [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: The chart has only circling minimums. Your learner sees the active runway early, has time for a normal approach and is cleared to land. Must he circle?
options: Yes, only the circling line may be used
No, he may land straight in as cleared
Yes, unless the tower waives the circle
No, but only if he flies a Category A airplane
final_quiz.why: Without straight-in minimums a straight-in landing is still allowed when the active runway is in sight in time for a normal approach and ATC has cleared the landing; pilots are not expected to circle, and should tell ATC if they want to [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20c]].

final_quiz.q: On base in a tailwind your learner will overshoot final and starts adding bank and bottom rudder. What is the safest action?
options: Add rudder to bring the nose around
Steepen to 45° and hold the altitude
Go around and set up again
Slip the turn with opposite rudder
final_quiz.why: Bank plus back pressure plus inside rudder sets up a skidding cross-control stall that may become a spin; the safest action for an overshoot is a go-around, with banks over 30° avoided at that height and no skidding turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

takeaways: Category is the speed you will fly: faster than your category means the higher line and the bigger area.
Read the whole circling line: MDA, HAA, visibility, the C symbol, a second set of minimums and every note.
Restrictions bind even under a clearance; at a non-towered field, use the 91.126(b) turn direction (left unless marked for right) unless a restriction requires otherwise.
Pick the pattern from airport layout, ceiling, visibility, wind, final course and ATC, then fly it tight enough to keep the airport in view.
Hold the MDA until in position to descend at a normal rate with normal maneuvers; seeing the runway is not enough.
Lost the airport: climbing turn toward the landing runway, then the missed approach course, with extra climb if needed.
Teach it on the ground, in the simulator and at altitude first; in the airplane, go around rather than skid an overshoot.
cfi_notes: Must or should: the IPH and the P/CG say the higher category minimums must be used when flying faster [[29:148|IPH 4-8]] [[34:305|AIM P/CG Aircraft approach category]], the AIM paragraph says should and calls it one acceptable method [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]], and the IFH says should [[23:42|IFH 1-23]]. Teach your learners to use the higher category every time.

Category basis: the IFH and the P/CG define category on 1.3 VSO only and say a Category A airplane circling in excess of 91 knots uses Category B [[23:42|IFH 1-23]] [[34:305|AIM P/CG Aircraft approach category]]. 14 CFR 97.3 uses VREF when specified, and 91 knots itself is already Category B [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]. Teach the regulation.

Radii: IPH Figure 4-2 lists only the old standard radii and IFH Figure 10-12 shows radii varying with category alone [[29:149|IPH 4-9]] [[23:311|IFH 10-20]], and the IPH's 2.86 NM Category C example compares with 2.8 NM in the AIM table for that MDA [[29:149|IPH 4-9]] [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]]. Teach from the AIM table and the C symbol.

Runway or airport in sight: the IFH says to keep visual contact with the runway of intended landing during the circle [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]; the rule requires an identifiable part of the airport to be distinctly visible [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]. Teach the rule as the legal floor and the IFH as technique.

Missed approach from a circle: the AIM says obstacle clearance is not necessarily provided by the published missed approach [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]], the IPH says it is not provided [[29:180|IPH 4-40]] [[29:181|IPH 4-41]]. Either way, teach extra climb inside the circling area before joining the track [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]].

The IPH's general IIMC advice is wings level, keep the heading and turn only to avoid known obstacles, with an immediate published missed approach during an instrument maneuver [[29:290|IPH A-4]]; for a circle the AIM gives the specific climbing turn toward the landing runway [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]]. Teach the AIM procedure for the circle.

The IPH calls the circling minimum a Circling Minimums Decision Altitude (CMDA) [[29:148|IPH 4-8]], but the regulation and the P/CG treat it as an MDA [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]] [[34:378|AIM P/CG Minimum descent altitude]]. Make sure learners do not treat it like a DA they may dip below while deciding.

How it is tested: the evaluator selects Tasks A and B combined with C, D or E, and circling does not apply to helicopters (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area VIII NOTE). In the PTS FSTD credit chart the circling approach is marked creditable only in the full flight simulator columns, while the nonprecision approach is also creditable in FTD levels 6 and 7 (FAA-S-8081-9E, Appendix 1). FSTD credit applies only under an approved part 141 or 142 curriculum (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). Application: be ready to explain which way to turn when the airport is lost, which radius applies, and exactly when the MDA may be left.

The IPH stabilized-approach heights for circling (stabilized by 500 ft above airport elevation or at the MDA, whichever is lower) are a turbojet standard; for propeller airplanes the IPH strongly recommends a stabilized approach without giving heights [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].
gaps: No source gives a bank angle, airspeed or pattern size for circling a light airplane; use the POH/AFM, the category speed and the radius.
The TPP page B2 with the radii table is not in the sources; the lesson uses the copy in AIM FIG 5-4-28.
No source gives a common-errors list for circling; the error table is built from AIM, IFH, IPH and AFH text.
The Instrument ACS is not in the build sources; the tolerances quoted come from the Instrument lesson IR.VI.D.
No source says how an instructor should simulate a loss of visual reference safely in the airplane; the lesson gives it only as Application advice.

activities.intro: Tap each situation, then tap the category minimums the learner must use.

items.t: No VREF; 1.3 VSO is 78 knots; circling at 85 knots
The same airplane circling at 95 knots in gusts
AIM example: a Category A airplane on a straight-in at 130 knots
AIM example: a Category B airplane circling at 145 knots
VREF 132 knots; flaps failed, circling at 150 knots

activities.why: Categories by speed: A under 91, B 91 to under 121, C 121 to under 141, D 141 to under 166 knots [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]. Faster than the category means the higher category's minimums [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]]; inoperative flaps are a listed reason [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

Circling with the stepdown fix identified
Airport elevation: HAA is measured from here
Missed approach: climb to 1300, then a climbing left turn
Time from the FAF to the MAP by groundspeed

activities.why: From the chart [[29:214|IPH Figure 4-45]]. The C symbol marks the expanded radii [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]]; HAA is the MDA's height above airport elevation [[34:356|AIM P/CG Height above airport]]; two sets of minimums serve pilots who can and cannot identify a fix [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20e]]; the time/distance table gives FAF to MAP times [[2:122|Chart Users' Guide p 122]].

activities.title: Circling numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Charlotte: Category A and B circling MDA 1320 ft, airport elevation 748 ft. What is the HAA?
items.why: 1320 - 748 = 572 ft, the HAA printed under the MDA [[29:214|IPH Figure 4-45]]; HAA is the height of the MDA above the published airport elevation [[34:356|AIM P/CG Height above airport]].

items.q: No VREF is published and VSO is 64 knots. What speed sets the approach category?
items.why: 1.3 x 64 = 83.2 knots, under 91 knots, so Category A [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]].

items.q: Expanded circling area, Category D, circling MDA 1,500 ft MSL. What is the radius?
items.why: The 1001-3000 ft row, Category D: 3.7 NM [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]].

items.q: About how many nautical miles is 1 statute mile of flight visibility? Give two decimals.
items.why: 5,280 / 6,076.1 = 0.87 NM [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]]. That is less than the 1.3 NM Category A radius [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]], so the radius is no target in low visibility.

items.q: At 165 knots groundspeed, how many feet larger is the turn radius at 20° of bank than at 30°?

activities.title: The airport disappears in the circle
activities.intro: Put the steps in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Recognize that no identifiable part of the airport is distinctly visible, and not just because of a normal bank
Climb pitch and climb power, then configure for the climb
Start the climbing turn toward the landing runway
Keep turning until established on the missed approach course
Reach a safe altitude before leaving the published missed approach
activities.why: Missed approach required [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]; climb pitch and power, configure, then the turn, with a call to ATC and a request for further clearance [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]; an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway, continued until established on the missed approach course [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]] [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21c]]; a safe altitude before leaving the published missed approach [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21g]].

activities.title: True or false: the visual part of the circle
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Featureless dark terrain around the airport tends to make a pilot fly a lower approach.
cards.why: True. It creates an illusion of greater height [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5a3(d)]].

cards.s: Bright runway lights with dark surroundings tend to make a pilot fly a lower approach.
cards.why: False. They create an illusion of less distance, leading to a higher approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5a3(f)]].

cards.s: An EFVS image can satisfy the need to see an identifiable part of the airport while circling.
cards.why: False. The references must be distinctly visible with natural vision throughout the circle [[29:161|IPH 4-21]].

cards.s: A skidding turn to fix an overshoot is acceptable if the bank stays under 30°.
cards.why: False. Do not make a skidding turn to correct an overshoot; go around [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

cards.s: Rain on the windscreen can create the illusion of greater height.
cards.why: True, and the pilot who does not recognize it flies a lower approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5a3(e)]].

activities.title: Teaching the circle, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are teaching an instrument learner circling approaches in a Category A trainer. The weather is good VMC and you are the safety pilot.

steps.s: On the ground he plans to fly the circle at 95 knots because of a gusty wind.
options: Brief the Category A line, since the airplane is certified Category A
Brief the Category B line, for the speed he will fly
Brief the straight-in line, since it is lower than the circling line
Brief the Category A line and add 100 ft for the gusts
steps.why: 95 knots is a Category B speed [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]; faster than the category means the higher category's minimums [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]].

steps.s: In the airplane, where does he first practice the workload of the circle?
options: In actual weather at the MDA, so it feels real
At night, when the runway lights are easy to see
At altitude, IFH circling patterns on an imaginary runway
Nowhere special; the first circle is the lesson
steps.why: The IFH circling approach patterns build the workload at a safe height [[23:193|IFH 7-32]], after simulator practice [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

steps.s: At the MDA you lift the view-limiting device. He sees the runway and wants to descend to pattern altitude at once on downwind.
options: Let him descend; the runway is distinctly visible
Have him descend 100 ft below the MDA to see better
Have him climb 300 ft and start the circle again
Hold the MDA until in position for a normal descent
steps.why: Leave the MDA only when continuously in a position to descend at a normal rate using normal maneuvers [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]].

steps.s: On downwind with a strong tailwind the runway is still distinctly visible, but the airplane is moving away from it fast.
options: Turn base early to allow for the high groundspeed
Fine, he is still inside the circling radius
Lower more flaps and keep flying the downwind
Descend a little to keep the airport in sight
steps.why: Downwind groundspeed can be much higher than indicated airspeed, so plan the turns to stay in the area [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c3]]; if the airport stops being distinctly visible, a missed approach is required [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]].

steps.s: On base he sees he will overshoot final and starts feeding in bottom rudder.
options: Coach more rudder to bring the nose around
Have him steepen to 45° to make the turn
Go around, then set up the circle again
Let him slip to final with crossed controls
steps.why: The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around; never skid the turn near the ground [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

steps.s: Back on the ground for the debrief.
options: Have him assess himself first, then compare with yours
List his errors, then give him a grade for the flight
Skip it; the flight went well enough overall
Grade only the landing, since that is what counts
steps.why: Collaborative assessment: the learner's self-assessment first, then a discussion that compares it with yours [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].
